    10→**📖 Documentation**: [Click here](docs/README.md)
    11→
    12→**sqlgen** is a modern, type-safe ORM and SQL query generator for C++20, inspired by Python's [SQLAlchemy](https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy)/[SQLModel](https://github.com/fastapi/sqlmodel) and Rust's [Diesel](https://github.com/diesel-rs/diesel). It provides a fluent, composable interface for database operations with compile-time type checking and SQL injection protection.
    13→
    14→sqlgen is based on and tightly integrated with [reflect-cpp](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp), a C++-20 library for fast serialization, deserialization and validation using reflection, similar to pydantic in Python, serde in Rust, encoding in Go or aeson in Haskell.
    15→
    16→Together, reflect-cpp and sqlgen enable reliable and efficient ETL pipelines.
    17→
    18→## Features
    19→
    20→- 🔒 **Type Safety**: Compile-time validation of table schemas and queries
    21→- 🛡️ **SQL Injection Protection**: Built-in input validation and parameterized queries
    22→- 🔄 **Composable Queries**: Fluent interface for building complex queries
    23→- 🚀 **High Performance**: Efficient batch operations and prepared statements
    24→- 📦 **Modern C++**: Leverages C++20 features for a clean, expressive API
    25→- 🔌 **Multiple Backends**: Support for PostgreSQL and SQLite
    26→- 🔍 **Reflection Integration**: Seamless integration with [reflect-cpp](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp) 
    27→
    28→## Supported databases 
    29→
    30→The following table lists the databases currently supported by sqlgen and the underlying libraries used:
    31→
    32→| Database      | Library                                                                  | Version      | License       | Remarks                                              |
    33→|---------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------|---------------| -----------------------------------------------------|
    34→| MySQL/MariaDB | [libmariadb](https://github.com/mariadb-corporation/mariadb-connector-c) | >= 3.4.5     | LGPL          |                                                      |
    35→| PostgreSQL    | [libpq](https://github.com/postgres/postgres)                            | >= 16.4      | PostgreSQL    | Will work for all libpq-compatible databases         |
    36→| sqlite        | [sqlite](https://sqlite.org/index.html)                                  | >= 3.49.1    | Public Domain |                                                      |
    37→
    38→## Quick Start
    39→
    40→### Installation using vcpkg
    41→
    42→1. Make sure you have the required dependencies installed (skip this step on Windows):
    43→```bash
    44→sudo apt-get install autoconf bison flex # Linux (Ubuntu, Debian, ...)
    45→brew install autoconf bison flex # macOS
    46→```
    47→
    48→2. Set up vcpkg:
    49→```bash
    50→git submodule update --init
    51→./vcpkg/bootstrap-vcpkg.sh  # Linux, macOS
    52→./vcpkg/bootstrap-vcpkg.bat # Windows
    53→```
    54→
    55→3. Build the library:
    56→```bash
    57→cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_CXX_STANDARD=20 -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
    58→cmake --build build -j 4  # gcc, clang
    59→cmake --build build --config Release -j 4  # MSVC
    60→```
    61→
    62→This will build the static library. To build the shared library 
    63→add `-DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON -DVCPKG_TARGET_TRIPLET=...` to the first line.
    64→Run `./vcpkg/vcpkg help triplets` to view all supported triplets. 
    65→Common triplets for shared libraries are `x64-linux-dynamic`, 
    66→`arm64-osx-dynamic` or `x64-osx-dynamic`.   
    67→
    68→Add `-DSQLGEN_MYSQL=ON` to support MySQL/MariaDB.
    69→
    70→4. Include in your CMake project:
    71→```cmake
    72→find_package(sqlgen REQUIRED)
    73→target_link_libraries(your_target PRIVATE sqlgen::sqlgen)
    74→```
    75→
    76→### Installation using Conan
    77→
    78→1. Install Conan (assuming you have Python and pipx installed):

    80→```bash

    83→```
    84→

1→# `sqlgen::PrimaryKey`
     2→
     3→`sqlgen::PrimaryKey` is used to indicate which key should be a primary key.
     4→
     5→## Usage
     6→
     7→### Basic Definition
     8→
     9→Define a primary key field in your struct:
    10→
    11→```cpp
    12→struct People {
    13→    sqlgen::PrimaryKey<std::string> first_name;
    14→    std::string last_name;
    15→    uint age;
    16→};
    17→```
    18→
    19→This generates the following SQL schema:
    20→
    21→```sql
    22→CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "People"(
    23→    "first_name" TEXT NOT NULL, 
    24→    "last_name"  TEXT NOT NULL, 
    25→    "age"        INTEGER NOT NULL,
    26→    PRIMARY_KEY("first_name")
    27→);
    28→```
    29→
    30→### Auto-incrementing Primary Keys
    31→
    32→You can define an auto-incrementing primary key by providing `sqlgen::auto_incr` as the second template argument to `sqlgen::PrimaryKey`. The underlying type of an auto-incrementing primary key must be an integral type.
    33→
    34→```cpp
    35→struct Person {
    36→  sqlgen::PrimaryKey<uint32_t, sqlgen::auto_incr> id;
    37→  std::string first_name;
    38→  std::string last_name;
    39→  int age;
    40→};
    41→```
    42→
    43→This will produce SQL schema with an auto-incrementing primary key. For instance, for PostgreSQL it will generate:
    44→
    45→```sql
    46→CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "Person"(
    47→    "id"         INTEGER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY,
    48→    "first_name" TEXT NOT NULL, 
    49→    "last_name"  TEXT NOT NULL, 
    50→    "age"        INTEGER NOT NULL,
    51→    PRIMARY KEY("id")
    52→);
    53→```
    54→
    55→And for SQLite:
    56→
    57→```sql
    58→CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "Person"(
    59→    "id"         INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, 
    60→    "first_name" TEXT NOT NULL, 
    61→    "last_name"  TEXT NOT NULL, 
    62→    "age"        INTEGER NOT NULL
    63→);
    64→```
    65→
    66→When you insert an object with an auto-incrementing primary key, you do not need to provide a value for the key field. The database will automatically assign a unique, incrementing value.
    67→
    68→```cpp
    69→auto homer = Person{.first_name = "Homer", .last_name = "Simpson", .age = 45};
    70→// The 'id' field is not set.
    71→
    72→// After writing to the database and reading it back, the 'id' will be populated.
    73→auto people = std::vector<Person>({homer});
    74→auto result = conn.and_then(sqlgen::write(std::ref(people)))
    75→                  .and_then(sqlgen::read<std::vector<Person>>())
    76→                  .value();
    77→
    78→// result[0].id will now have a value, for instance 1.
    79→```
    80→
    81→### Assignment and Access
    82→
    83→Assign values to primary key fields:
    84→
    85→```cpp
    86→const auto person = People{
    87→    .first_name = "Homer",
    88→    .last_name = "Simpson",
    89→    .age = 45
    90→};
    91→```
    92→
    93→Access the underlying value using any of these methods:
    94→
    95→```cpp
    96→person.first_name();
    97→person.first_name.get();
    98→person.first_name.value();
    99→```
   100→
   101→## Notes
   102→
   103→- The template parameter specifies the type of the primary key field
   104→- Primary key fields are automatically marked as NOT NULL in the generated SQL
   105→- Auto-incrementing primary keys must have an integral type.
   106→- The class supports:
   107→  - Direct value assignment
   108→  - Multiple access methods for the underlying value
   109→  - Reflection for SQL operations
   110→  - Move and copy semantics
   111→- Primary keys can be used with any supported SQL data type

    10→**📖 Documentation**: [Click here](docs/README.md)
    11→
    12→**sqlgen** is a modern, type-safe ORM and SQL query generator for C++20, inspired by Python's [SQLAlchemy](https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy)/[SQLModel](https://github.com/fastapi/sqlmodel) and Rust's [Diesel](https://github.com/diesel-rs/diesel). It provides a fluent, composable interface for database operations with compile-time type checking and SQL injection protection.
    13→
    14→sqlgen is based on and tightly integrated with [reflect-cpp](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp), a C++-20 library for fast serialization, deserialization and validation using reflection, similar to pydantic in Python, serde in Rust, encoding in Go or aeson in Haskell.
    15→
    16→Together, reflect-cpp and sqlgen enable reliable and efficient ETL pipelines.
    17→
    18→## Features
    19→
    20→- 🔒 **Type Safety**: Compile-time validation of table schemas and queries
    21→- 🛡️ **SQL Injection Protection**: Built-in input validation and parameterized queries
    22→- 🔄 **Composable Queries**: Fluent interface for building complex queries
    23→- 🚀 **High Performance**: Efficient batch operations and prepared statements
    24→- 📦 **Modern C++**: Leverages C++20 features for a clean, expressive API
    25→- 🔌 **Multiple Backends**: Support for PostgreSQL and SQLite
    26→- 🔍 **Reflection Integration**: Seamless integration with [reflect-cpp](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp) 
    27→
    28→## Supported databases 
    29→
    30→The following table lists the databases currently supported by sqlgen and the underlying libraries used:
    31→
    32→| Database      | Library                                                                  | Version      | License       | Remarks                                              |
    33→|---------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------|---------------| -----------------------------------------------------|
    34→| MySQL/MariaDB | [libmariadb](https://github.com/mariadb-corporation/mariadb-connector-c) | >= 3.4.5     | LGPL          |                                                      |
    35→| PostgreSQL    | [libpq](https://github.com/postgres/postgres)                            | >= 16.4      | PostgreSQL    | Will work for all libpq-compatible databases         |
    36→| sqlite        | [sqlite](https://sqlite.org/index.html)                                  | >= 3.49.1    | Public Domain |                                                      |
    37→
    38→## Quick Start
    39→
    40→### Installation using vcpkg
    41→
    42→1. Make sure you have the required dependencies installed (skip this step on Windows):
    43→```bash
    44→sudo apt-get install autoconf bison flex # Linux (Ubuntu, Debian, ...)
    45→brew install autoconf bison flex # macOS
    46→```
    47→
    48→2. Set up vcpkg:
    49→```bash
    50→git submodule update --init
    51→./vcpkg/bootstrap-vcpkg.sh  # Linux, macOS
    52→./vcpkg/bootstrap-vcpkg.bat # Windows
    53→```
    54→
    55→3. Build the library:
    56→```bash
    57→cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_CXX_STANDARD=20 -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
    58→cmake --build build -j 4  # gcc, clang
    59→cmake --build build --config Release -j 4  # MSVC
    60→```
    61→
    62→This will build the static library. To build the shared library 
    63→add `-DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON -DVCPKG_TARGET_TRIPLET=...` to the first line.
    64→Run `./vcpkg/vcpkg help triplets` to view all supported triplets. 
    65→Common triplets for shared libraries are `x64-linux-dynamic`, 
    66→`arm64-osx-dynamic` or `x64-osx-dynamic`.   
    67→
    68→Add `-DSQLGEN_MYSQL=ON` to support MySQL/MariaDB.
    69→
    70→4. Include in your CMake project:
    71→```cmake
    72→find_package(sqlgen REQUIRED)
    73→target_link_libraries(your_target PRIVATE sqlgen::sqlgen)
    74→```
    75→
    76→### Installation using Conan
    77→
    78→1. Install Conan (assuming you have Python and pipx installed):
    79→
    80→```bash
    81→pipx install conan
    82→conan profile detect
    83→```
    84→
    85→For older versions of pip, you can also use `pip` instead of `pipx`.
    86→
    87→2. Build the library:
    88→
    89→```bash
    90→conan build . --build=missing -s compiler.cppstd=gnu20
    91→```
    92→
    93→This will build the static library. To build the shared library,
    94→add `-o */*:shared=True`. 
    95→
    96→Add `-o sqlgen/*:with_mysql=True` to support MySQL/MariaDB.
    97→
    98→3. Include in your CMake project:
    99→```cmake

   101→target_link_libraries(your_target PRIVATE sqlgen::sqlgen)
   102→```
   103→
   104→You can call `conan inspect .` to get an overview of the supported options.
   105→
   106→## Usage Examples
   107→
   108→### Hello World
   109→
   110→```cpp
   111→#include <sqlgen/sqlite.hpp>
   112→#include <iostream>
   113→
   114→struct User {
   115→    std::string name;
   116→    int age;
   117→};
   118→
   119→int main() {
   120→    // Connect to SQLite database
   121→    const auto conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("test.db");
   122→    
   123→    // Create and insert a user
   124→    const auto user = User{.name = "John", .age = 30};
   125→    sqlgen::write(conn, user);
   126→    
   127→    // Read all users
   128→    const auto users = sqlgen::read<std::vector<User>>(conn).value();
   129→    
   130→    for (const auto& u : users) {
   131→        std::cout << u.name << " is " << u.age << " years old\n";
   132→    }
   133→}
   134→```
   135→
   136→### Connecting to a Database
   137→
   138→```cpp
   139→#include <sqlgen/postgres.hpp>
   140→
   141→// PostgreSQL connection
   142→const auto credentials = sqlgen::postgres::Credentials{
   143→    .user = "username",
   144→    .password = "password",
   145→    .host = "localhost",
   146→    .dbname = "mydb",
   147→    .port = 5432
   148→};
   149→
   150→const auto conn = sqlgen::postgres::connect(credentials);
   151→
   152→// SQLite connection
   153→const auto sqlite_conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("database.db");
   154→```
   155→
   156→### Defining Models
   157→
   158→```cpp
   159→struct Person {
   160→    std::string first_name;
   161→    std::string last_name;
   162→    uint32_t age;
   163→    std::optional<std::string> email;  // Nullable field
   164→};
   165→```
   166→
   167→### Inserting Data
   168→
   169→```cpp
   170→const auto people = std::vector<Person>({
   171→    Person{.first_name = "Homer", .last_name = "Simpson", .age = 45},
   172→    Person{.first_name = "Marge", .last_name = "Simpson", .age = 42}
   173→});
   174→
   175→// Automatically creates table if it doesn't exist
   176→// (recall that the table is fully defined at compile time)
   177→const auto result = sqlgen::write(conn, people);
   178→
   179→if (!result) {
   180→    std::cerr << "Error: " << result.error().what() << std::endl;
   181→}
   182→```
   183→

   186→```cpp
   187→...
   188→
   189→// write(...) abstracts these steps away, but

   191→// can use sqlgen::insert.
   192→const auto result = begin_transaction(conn)
   193→                        .and_then(create_table<Person> | if_not_exists)
   194→                        .and_then(insert(std::ref(people)))
   195→                        .and_then(commit);
   196→
   197→...

1→# `sqlgen::create_table` 
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen::create_table` interface provides a type-safe way to create tables in a SQL database. It supports the `if_not_exists` clause to handle cases where the table may already exist.
     4→
     5→## Usage
     6→
     7→### Basic Create Table
     8→
     9→Create a table:
    10→
    11→```cpp
    12→const auto conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("database.db");
    13→
    14→sqlgen::create_table<Person>(conn).value();
    15→```
    16→
    17→This generates the following SQL:
    18→
    19→```sql
    20→CREATE TABLE "Person" ("id" INTEGER NOT NULL, "first_name" TEXT NOT NULL, "last_name" TEXT NOT NULL, "age" INTEGER NOT NULL);
    21→```
    22→
    23→Note that `conn` is actually a connection wrapped into an `sqlgen::Result<...>`.
    24→This means you can use monadic error handling and fit this into a single line:
    25→
    26→```cpp
    27→// sqlgen::Result<Ref<Connection>>
    28→const auto result = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("database.db").and_then(
    29→                        sqlgen::create_table<Person>);
    30→```
    31→
    32→Please refer to the documentation on `sqlgen::Result<...>` for more information on error handling.
    33→
    34→### With `if_not_exists` clause
    35→
    36→Create a table only if it doesn't exist:
    37→
    38→```cpp
    39→using namespace sqlgen;
    40→
    41→const auto query = create_table<Person> | if_not_exists;
    42→
    43→query(conn).value();
    44→```
    45→
    46→This generates the following SQL:
    47→
    48→```sql
    49→CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "Person" ("id" INTEGER NOT NULL, "first_name" TEXT NOT NULL, "last_name" TEXT NOT NULL, "age" INTEGER NOT NULL);
    50→```
    51→
    52→You can also use monadic error handling here:
    53→
    54→```cpp
    55→using namespace sqlgen;
    56→
    57→const auto query = create_table<Person> | if_not_exists;
    58→
    59→// sqlgen::Result<Ref<Connection>>
    60→const auto result = sqlite::connect("database.db").and_then(query);
    61→```
    62→
    63→## Example: Full Query Composition
    64→
    65→```cpp
    66→using namespace sqlgen;
    67→
    68→const auto query = create_table<Person> | if_not_exists;
    69→
    70→const auto result = query(conn);
    71→
    72→if (!result) {
    73→    // Error handling
    74→}
    75→```
    76→
    77→This generates the following SQL:
    78→
    79→```sql
    80→CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "Person" ("id" INTEGER NOT NULL, "first_name" TEXT NOT NULL, "last_name" TEXT NOT NULL, "age" INTEGER NOT NULL);
    81→```
    82→
    83→It is strongly recommended that you use `using namespace sqlgen`. However,
    84→if you do not want to do that, you can rewrite the example above as follows:
    85→
    86→```cpp
    87→const auto query = sqlgen::create_table<Person> | sqlgen::if_not_exists;
    88→
    89→const auto result = query(conn);
    90→```
    91→
    92→## Notes
    93→
    94→- The `if_not_exists` clause is optional - if omitted, the query will fail if the table already exists
    95→- The `Result<Ref<Connection>>` type provides error handling; use `.value()` to extract the result (will throw an exception if there's an error) or handle errors as needed or refer to the documentation on `sqlgen::Result<...>` for other forms of error handling.
    96→- The table name is derived from the struct name (e.g., `Person` becomes `"Person"` in SQL)
    97→- Column types are automatically mapped from C++ types:
    98→  - `std::string` → `TEXT`
    99→  - `int`/`int32_t` → `INTEGER`
   100→  - `uint32_t` → `INTEGER`
   101→  - `std::optional<T>` → nullable column of type T
   102→  - `sqlgen::PrimaryKey<T>` → column of type T with PRIMARY KEY constraint
   103→- All columns are NOT NULL by default unless they are `std::optional`
   104→

    10→namespace sqlgen {

    13→  requires is_connection<Connection>
    14→Result<Ref<Connection>> exec(const Ref<Connection>& _conn,
    15→                             const std::string& _sql) {
    16→  return _conn->execute(_sql).transform([&](const auto&) { return _conn; });

    21→Result<Ref<Connection>> exec(const Result<Ref<Connection>>& _res,
    22→                             const std::string& _sql) {

    30→};

1→# `sqlgen::group_by` and Aggregations
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen::group_by` interface provides a type-safe way to group and aggregate data in SQL queries. It supports various aggregation functions like `count`, `avg`, `sum`, `min`, `max`, and `count_distinct`.
     4→
     5→## Usage
     6→
     7→### Basic Aggregations
     8→
     9→Perform aggregations without grouping:
    10→
    11→```cpp
    12→using namespace sqlgen;
    13→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    14→
    15→struct Children {
    16→    int num_children;
    17→    int num_last_names;
    18→    double avg_age;
    19→    double max_age;
    20→    double min_age;
    21→    double sum_age;
    22→};
    23→
    24→const auto get_children = select_from<Person>(
    25→    avg("age"_c).as<"avg_age">(),
    26→    count().as<"num_children">(),
    27→    max("age"_c).as<"max_age">(),
    28→    min("age"_c).as<"min_age">(),
    29→    sum("age"_c).as<"sum_age">(),
    30→    count_distinct("last_name"_c).as<"num_last_names">()
    31→) | where("age"_c < 18) | to<Children>;
    32→
    33→const auto children = sqlite::connect()
    34→    .and_then(get_children)
    35→    .value();
    36→```
    37→
    38→This generates the following SQL:
    39→
    40→```sql
    41→SELECT 
    42→    AVG("age") as "avg_age",
    43→    COUNT(*) as "num_children",
    44→    MAX("age") as "max_age",
    45→    MIN("age") as "min_age",
    46→    SUM("age") as "sum_age",
    47→    COUNT(DISTINCT "last_name") as "num_last_names"
    48→FROM "Person"
    49→WHERE "age" < 18;
    50→```
    51→
    52→### Group By with Aggregations
    53→
    54→Group data and perform aggregations:
    55→
    56→```cpp
    57→using namespace sqlgen;
    58→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    59→
    60→struct Children {
    61→    std::string last_name;
    62→    int num_children;
    63→    int num_last_names;
    64→    double avg_age;
    65→    double max_age;
    66→    double min_age;
    67→    double sum_age;
    68→};
    69→
    70→const auto get_children = select_from<Person>(
    71→    "last_name"_c,
    72→    avg("age"_c).as<"avg_age">(),
    73→    count().as<"num_children">(),
    74→    max("age"_c).as<"max_age">(),
    75→    min("age"_c).as<"min_age">(),
    76→    sum("age"_c).as<"sum_age">(),
    77→    count_distinct("last_name"_c).as<"num_last_names">()
    78→) | where("age"_c < 18) | group_by("last_name"_c) | to<std::vector<Children>>;
    79→
    80→const auto children = sqlite::connect()
    81→    .and_then(drop<Person> | if_exists)
    82→    .and_then(write(std::ref(people)))
    83→    .and_then(get_children)
    84→    .value();
    85→```
    86→
    87→This generates the following SQL:
    88→
    89→```sql
    90→SELECT 
    91→    "last_name",
    92→    AVG("age") as "avg_age",
    93→    COUNT(*) as "num_children",
    94→    MAX("age") as "max_age",
    95→    MIN("age") as "min_age",
    96→    SUM("age") as "sum_age",
    97→    COUNT(DISTINCT "last_name") as "num_last_names"
    98→FROM "Person"
    99→WHERE "age" < 18
   100→GROUP BY "last_name";
   101→```
   102→
   103→## Available Aggregation Functions
   104→
   105→The following aggregation functions are available:
   106→
   107→- `count()` - Counts all rows
   108→- `count_distinct(col)` - Counts distinct values in a column
   109→- `avg(col)` - Calculates average of a column
   110→- `sum(col)` - Calculates sum of a column
   111→- `max(col)` - Finds maximum value in a column
   112→- `min(col)` - Finds minimum value in a column
   113→
   114→Each aggregation function can be aliased using the `.as<"alias">()` syntax.
   115→
   116→## Aggregating Nullable Values
   117→
   118→When working with nullable columns (e.g., `std::optional<T>`), it's important to understand how aggregations handle null values:
   119→
   120→1. The result of aggregating a nullable column must also be nullable (e.g., `std::optional<double>`)
   121→2. Null values are excluded from aggregation calculations
   122→3. If all values in a group are null, the aggregation result will be null
   123→
   124→### Example with Nullable Values
   125→
   126→```cpp
   127→struct Person {
   128→    sqlgen::PrimaryKey<uint32_t> id;
   129→    std::string first_name;
   130→    std::string last_name;
   131→    std::optional<double> age;  // Nullable age field
   132→};
   133→
   134→struct Children {
   135→    int num_children;           // Non-nullable count
   136→    int num_last_names;        // Non-nullable count
   137→    std::optional<double> avg_age;  // Nullable aggregation
   138→    std::optional<double> max_age;  // Nullable aggregation
   139→    std::optional<double> min_age;  // Nullable aggregation
   140→    std::optional<double> sum_age;  // Nullable aggregation
   141→};
   142→
   143→const auto get_children = select_from<Person>(
   144→    avg("age"_c).as<"avg_age">(),      // Results in std::optional<double>
   145→    count().as<"num_children">(),      // Results in int (non-nullable)
   146→    max("age"_c).as<"max_age">(),      // Results in std::optional<double>
   147→    min("age"_c).as<"min_age">(),      // Results in std::optional<double>
   148→    sum("age"_c).as<"sum_age">(),      // Results in std::optional<double>
   149→    count_distinct("last_name"_c).as<"num_last_names">()
   150→) | where("age"_c < 18 or "age"_c.is_null()) | to<Children>;
   151→```
   152→
   153→In this example:
   154→- The `age` column is nullable (`std::optional<double>`)
   155→- All aggregations of `age` result in nullable values (`std::optional<double>`)
   156→- The `count()` and `count_distinct()` functions return non-nullable integers
   157→- The `where` clause includes both non-null values less than 18 and null values
   158→- If all values in a group are null, the aggregation results (avg, max, min, sum) will be null
   159→
   160→### Important Notes
   161→
   162→- Always use nullable types (`std::optional<T>`) for aggregated values when the source column is nullable
   163→- Count operations (`count()`, `count_distinct()`) always return non-nullable integers
   164→- Null values are excluded from aggregation calculations (avg, sum, max, min)
   165→- When all values in a group are null, the aggregation result will be null
   166→- The type system will enforce these rules at compile time
   167→
   168→## The `.as` Operator
   169→
   170→The `.as` operator allows you to alias columns and expressions in your SQL queries. This is particularly important when mapping query results to C++ structs, as the field names in your struct must match the aliases used in the query.
   171→
   172→### Usage
   173→
   174→You can use `.as` in several ways:
   175→
   176→```cpp
   177→// Method 1: Using the .as() member function
   178→"field1"_c.as<"field">()
   179→
   180→// Method 2: Using the pipe operator with as
   181→"nullable"_c | as<"nullable_field">
   182→
   183→// Method 3: Using as directly with values
   184→as<"one">(1)
   185→"hello" | as<"hello">
   186→```
   187→
   188→### Important Notes
   189→
   190→- Field names in your result struct must exactly match the aliases used in the query
   191→- Fields are matched by name, not by order
   192→- You can alias any column, expression, or literal value
   193→- The alias must be a string literal (using the `as<"alias">` syntax)
   194→
   195→### Example
   196→
   197→```cpp
   198→struct Result {
   199→    std::string field;           // Matches "field1"_c.as<"field">()
   200→    double avg_field2;           // Matches avg("field2"_c).as<"avg_field2">()
   201→    std::optional<std::string> nullable_field;  // Matches "nullable"_c | as<"nullable_field">
   202→    int one;                     // Matches as<"one">(1)
   203→    std::string hello;           // Matches "hello" | as<"hello">
   204→};
   205→
   206→const auto query = select_from<TestTable>(
   207→    "field1"_c.as<"field">(),
   208→    avg("field2"_c).as<"avg_field2">(),
   209→    "nullable"_c | as<"nullable_field">,
   210→    as<"one">(1),
   211→    "hello" | as<"hello">
   212→) | to<Result>;
   213→```
   214→
   215→In this example, each field in the `Result` struct must have a name that matches one of the aliases used in the query. The order of the fields in the struct doesn't matter, but the names must match exactly.
   216→
   217→## Notes
   218→
   219→- The `group_by` clause must be used before `order_by` or `limit` clauses
   220→- You cannot use `group_by` multiple times in the same query
   221→- Aggregation functions can be used with or without `group_by`
   222→- The result type must match the structure of your select statement. Note that fields are matched by name, not order.
   223→- All aggregations are type-safe and will map to appropriate SQL types
   224→- The `Result<...>` type provides error handling; use `.value()` to extract the result (will throw an exception if there's an error) or handle errors as needed
   225→

    17→namespace sqlgen {

    19→/// The concept any connection needs to implements.
    20→template <class ConnType>
    21→concept is_connection = requires(
    22→    ConnType c, std::string _sql, dynamic::Statement _stmt,
    23→    dynamic::SelectFrom _select_from, dynamic::Insert _insert,
    24→    const dynamic::Write& _write, std::vector<internal::MockTable> _data) {
    25→  /// Begins a transaction.
    26→  { c.begin_transaction() } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    27→
    28→  /// Commits a transaction.
    29→  { c.commit() } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    30→
    31→  /// Executes a statement.
    32→  { c.execute(_sql) } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    33→
    34→  /// Inserts data into the database using the INSERT statement.
    35→  /// More minimal approach than write, but can be used inside transactions.
    36→  {
    37→    c.insert(_insert, _data.begin(), _data.end())
    38→  } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    39→
    40→  /// Reads the results of a SelectFrom statement.
    41→  {
    42→    c.template read<std::vector<internal::MockTable>>(_select_from)
    43→  } -> std::same_as<Result<std::vector<internal::MockTable>>>;
    44→
    45→  /// Commits a transaction.
    46→  { c.rollback() } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    47→
    48→  /// Transpiles a statement to a particular SQL dialect.
    49→  { c.to_sql(_stmt) } -> std::same_as<std::string>;
    50→
    51→  /// Starts the write operation.
    52→  { c.start_write(_write) } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    53→
    54→  /// Ends the write operation and thus commits the results.
    55→  { c.end_write() } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    56→
    57→  /// Writes data into a table.
    58→  { c.write(_data.begin(), _data.end()) } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    59→};
    60→
    61→}  // namespace sqlgen

1→# `sqlgen::Result`
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen::Result` type provides a way to handle errors without exceptions in sqlgen. It is an alias for `rfl::Result` and is used throughout sqlgen's API to handle potential failures in database operations.
     4→
     5→Note that `sqlgen::Result` and `rfl::Result` are deliberately designed
     6→to resemble C++ 23's [std::expected](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/utility/expected).
     7→
     8→## Usage
     9→
    10→### Basic Usage
    11→
    12→Handle database operations that might fail:
    13→
    14→```cpp
    15→// Reading from database
    16→const auto people = sqlgen::read<std::vector<Person>>(conn);
    17→
    18→if (people) {
    19→    // Success case - use the value
    20→    const auto& result = *people;
    21→} else {
    22→    // Error case - handle the error
    23→    const auto& error = people.error();
    24→}
    25→
    26→// Writing to database
    27→const auto write_result = sqlgen::write(conn, data);
    28→
    29→if (!write_result) {
    30→    // Handle write error
    31→    const auto& error = write_result.error();
    32→}
    33→```
    34→
    35→### Monadic Operations
    36→
    37→The `Result` type supports several monadic operations for chaining operations:
    38→
    39→```cpp
    40→// Transform values (T -> U)
    41→const auto count = result.transform([](const auto& people) {
    42→    return people.size();
    43→});
    44→
    45→// Chain operations that might fail (T -> Result<U>)
    46→const auto processed = result.and_then([](const auto& people) {
    47→    return process_people(people);  // Returns Result<ProcessedData>
    48→});
    49→
    50→// Handle errors with alternative computation (Error -> Result<T>)
    51→const auto recovered = result.or_else([](const auto& error) {
    52→    return fallback_operation();  // Returns Result<T>
    53→});
    54→```
    55→
    56→### Value Access Methods
    57→
    58→Multiple ways to safely access the contained value:

1→# `sqlgen::exec`
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen::exec` interface provides a way to execute raw SQL statements on a database connection. It's useful when you need to perform database operations that aren't covered by the type-safe interfaces, such as setting database-specific parameters or executing custom SQL statements.
     4→
     5→## Usage
     6→
     7→### Basic Execution
     8→
     9→Execute a raw SQL statement:
    10→
    11→```cpp
    12→const auto conn = sqlgen::postgres::connect(credentials);
    13→
    14→sqlgen::exec(conn, "SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';").value();
    15→```
    16→
    17→### Curried Execution
    18→
    19→You can also use a curried version of `exec` that takes the SQL statement first and returns a function that accepts the connection. This is useful for chaining operations:
    20→
    21→```cpp
    22→using namespace sqlgen;
    23→
    24→const auto query = exec("SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';");
    25→
    26→// Using with a connection reference
    27→const auto conn = postgres::connect(credentials);
    28→query(conn).value();
    29→
    30→// Or in a chain with other operations
    31→postgres::connect(credentials)
    32→    .and_then(exec("SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';"))
    33→    .value();
    34→```
    35→
    36→## Example: Full Query Composition
    37→
    38→Here's a complete example showing how to use `exec` within a chain of operations:
    39→
    40→```cpp
    41→using namespace sqlgen;
    42→
    43→const auto result = postgres::connect(credentials)
    44→    .and_then(exec("SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';"))
    45→    .and_then(drop<Person> | if_exists)
    46→    .and_then(write(people))
    47→    .and_then(read<std::vector<Person>>)
    48→    .value();
    49→```
    50→
    51→This executes the following SQL statements in sequence:
    52→
    53→```sql
    54→SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';
    55→DROP TABLE IF EXISTS "Person";
    56→-- Table creation and data insertion via write
    57→-- Data retrieval via read
    58→```
    59→
    60→## Notes
    61→
    62→- The `Result<Ref<Connection>>` type provides error handling; use `.value()` to extract the result (will throw an exception if there's an error) or handle errors as needed
    63→- The function has two overloads:
    64→  1. Takes a connection reference and SQL string
    65→  2. Takes a `Result<Ref<Connection>>` and SQL string
    66→- The curried version is particularly useful when you want to:
    67→  - Chain multiple database operations together
    68→  - Pass the execution operation as a function to other operations
    69→- Use `exec` when you need to:
    70→  - Execute database-specific commands
    71→  - Set database parameters
    72→  - Run custom SQL statements not covered by type-safe interfaces
    73→  - Perform administrative tasks
    74→- Exercise caution when using `exec` with user-provided input to prevent SQL injection attacks
    75→- The SQL statement is executed as-is, so ensure it's compatible with your database dialect

    17→namespace sqlgen {

    19→/// The concept any connection needs to implements.
    20→template <class ConnType>
    21→concept is_connection = requires(
    22→    ConnType c, std::string _sql, dynamic::Statement _stmt,
    23→    dynamic::SelectFrom _select_from, dynamic::Insert _insert,
    24→    const dynamic::Write& _write, std::vector<internal::MockTable> _data) {
    25→  /// Begins a transaction.
    26→  { c.begin_transaction() } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    27→
    28→  /// Commits a transaction.
    29→  { c.commit() } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    30→
    31→  /// Executes a statement.
    32→  { c.execute(_sql) } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    33→
    34→  /// Inserts data into the database using the INSERT statement.
    35→  /// More minimal approach than write, but can be used inside transactions.
    36→  {
    37→    c.insert(_insert, _data.begin(), _data.end())
    38→  } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    39→
    40→  /// Reads the results of a SelectFrom statement.
    41→  {
    42→    c.template read<std::vector<internal::MockTable>>(_select_from)
    43→  } -> std::same_as<Result<std::vector<internal::MockTable>>>;
    44→
    45→  /// Commits a transaction.
    46→  { c.rollback() } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    47→
    48→  /// Transpiles a statement to a particular SQL dialect.
    49→  { c.to_sql(_stmt) } -> std::same_as<std::string>;
    50→
    51→  /// Starts the write operation.
    52→  { c.start_write(_write) } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    53→
    54→  /// Ends the write operation and thus commits the results.
    55→  { c.end_write() } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    56→
    57→  /// Writes data into a table.
    58→  { c.write(_data.begin(), _data.end()) } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    59→};

1→# Transactions
     2→
     3→sqlgen provides a simple and safe way to handle database transactions. Transactions ensure that a series of database operations are executed atomically - either all operations succeed, or none of them do.
     4→
     5→## Basic Usage
     6→
     7→Transactions in sqlgen are managed through three main functions:
     8→
     9→- `sqlgen::begin_transaction` - Starts a new transaction
    10→- `sqlgen::commit` - Commits the current transaction
    11→- `sqlgen::rollback` - Rolls back the current transaction 
    12→
    13→Here's a basic example of how to use transactions:
    14→
    15→```cpp
    16→using namespace sqlgen;
    17→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    18→
    19→// Start a transaction and chain operations
    20→// Note that all of these operations return
    21→// the connection if they are successful.
    22→auto conn = sqlite::connect("database.db")
    23→            .and_then(begin_transaction)
    24→            .and_then(delete_from<Person> | where("first_name"_c == "Hugo"))
    25→            .and_then(update<Person>("age"_c.set(46)) | where("first_name"_c == "Homer"))
    26→            .and_then(commit);
    27→```
    28→
    29→## Automatic Rollback
    30→
    31→sqlgen provides automatic rollback protection through RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization). `begin_transaction` creates a `sqlgen::Transaction` object. If a transaction is not explicitly committed, it will be automatically rolled back when the transaction object goes out of scope. This helps ensure database consistency.
    32→
    33→## Error Handling
    34→
    35→All transaction operations return a `sqlgen::Result<Ref<Connection>>`, which allows for safe error handling and operation chaining. If any operation in the transaction chain fails, the error will be propagated through the Result type, and the transaction will be rolled back.
    36→
    37→Example with error handling:
    38→
    39→```cpp
    40→using namespace sqlgen;
    41→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    42→
    43→auto conn = sqlite::connect("database.db")
    44→            .and_then(begin_transaction)
    45→            .and_then(delete_from<Person> | where("first_name"_c == "Hugo"))
    46→            .and_then(update<Person>("age"_c.set(46)) | where("first_name"_c == "Homer"))
    47→            .and_then(commit);
    48→
    49→if (!conn) {
    50→    // Handle error
    51→    std::cerr << "Transaction failed: " << result.error() << std::endl;
    52→    return;
    53→}
    54→
    55→// Transaction was successful. conn contains the active connection.
    56→```
    57→
    58→## Best Practices
    59→
    60→1. Chain operations using `.and_then()` to maintain transaction context
    61→2. Let the automatic rollback handle cleanup in case of errors
    62→3. Check the Result type after transaction operations to handle any errors
    63→4. Keep transactions as short as possible to minimize lock contention

    12→**sqlgen** is a modern, type-safe ORM and SQL query generator for C++20, inspired by Python's [SQLAlchemy](https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy)/[SQLModel](https://github.com/fastapi/sqlmodel) and Rust's [Diesel](https://github.com/diesel-rs/diesel). It provides a fluent, composable interface for database operations with compile-time type checking and SQL injection protection.
    13→
    14→sqlgen is based on and tightly integrated with [reflect-cpp](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp), a C++-20 library for fast serialization, deserialization and validation using reflection, similar to pydantic in Python, serde in Rust, encoding in Go or aeson in Haskell.
    15→
    16→Together, reflect-cpp and sqlgen enable reliable and efficient ETL pipelines.
    17→
    18→## Features
    19→
    20→- 🔒 **Type Safety**: Compile-time validation of table schemas and queries
    21→- 🛡️ **SQL Injection Protection**: Built-in input validation and parameterized queries
    22→- 🔄 **Composable Queries**: Fluent interface for building complex queries
    23→- 🚀 **High Performance**: Efficient batch operations and prepared statements
    24→- 📦 **Modern C++**: Leverages C++20 features for a clean, expressive API
    25→- 🔌 **Multiple Backends**: Support for PostgreSQL and SQLite
    26→- 🔍 **Reflection Integration**: Seamless integration with [reflect-cpp](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp)

It provides a fluent, composable interface for database operations with compile-time type checking and SQL injection protection.
    13→
    14→sqlgen is based on and tightly integrated with [reflect-cpp](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp), a C++-20 library for fast serialization, deserialization and validation using reflection, similar to pydantic in Python, serde in Rust, encoding in Go or aeson in Haskell.
    15→

    17→
    18→## Features

1→# `sqlgen::exec`
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen::exec` interface provides a way to execute raw SQL statements on a database connection. It's useful when you need to perform database operations that aren't covered by the type-safe interfaces, such as setting database-specific parameters or executing custom SQL statements.
     4→
     5→## Usage
     6→
     7→### Basic Execution
     8→
     9→Execute a raw SQL statement:
    10→
    11→```cpp
    12→const auto conn = sqlgen::postgres::connect(credentials);
    13→
    14→sqlgen::exec(conn, "SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';").value();
    15→```
    16→
    17→### Curried Execution
    18→
    19→You can also use a curried version of `exec` that takes the SQL statement first and returns a function that accepts the connection. This is useful for chaining operations:
    20→
    21→```cpp
    22→using namespace sqlgen;
    23→
    24→const auto query = exec("SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';");
    25→
    26→// Using with a connection reference
    27→const auto conn = postgres::connect(credentials);
    28→query(conn).value();
    29→
    30→// Or in a chain with other operations
    31→postgres::connect(credentials)
    32→    .and_then(exec("SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';"))
    33→    .value();
    34→```
    35→
    36→## Example: Full Query Composition
    37→
    38→Here's a complete example showing how to use `exec` within a chain of operations:
    39→
    40→```cpp
    41→using namespace sqlgen;
    42→
    43→const auto result = postgres::connect(credentials)
    44→    .and_then(exec("SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';"))
    45→    .and_then(drop<Person> | if_exists)
    46→    .and_then(write(people))
    47→    .and_then(read<std::vector<Person>>)
    48→    .value();
    49→```
    50→
    51→This executes the following SQL statements in sequence:
    52→
    53→```sql
    54→SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';
    55→DROP TABLE IF EXISTS "Person";
    56→-- Table creation and data insertion via write
    57→-- Data retrieval via read
    58→```
    59→
    60→## Notes
    61→
    62→- The `Result<Ref<Connection>>` type provides error handling; use `.value()` to extract the result (will throw an exception if there's an error) or handle errors as needed
    63→- The function has two overloads:
    64→  1. Takes a connection reference and SQL string
    65→  2. Takes a `Result<Ref<Connection>>` and SQL string
    66→- The curried version is particularly useful when you want to:
    67→  - Chain multiple database operations together
    68→  - Pass the execution operation as a function to other operations
    69→- Use `exec` when you need to:
    70→  - Execute database-specific commands
    71→  - Set database parameters
    72→  - Run custom SQL statements not covered by type-safe interfaces
    73→  - Perform administrative tasks
    74→- Exercise caution when using `exec` with user-provided input to prevent SQL injection attacks
    75→- The SQL statement is executed as-is, so ensure it's compatible with your database dialect
    76→

1→# `sqlgen::drop` 
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen::drop` interface provides a type-safe way to drop tables from a SQL database. It supports the `if_exists` clause to handle cases where the table may not exist.
     4→
     5→## Usage
     6→
     7→### Basic Drop
     8→
     9→Drop a table:
    10→
    11→```cpp
    12→const auto conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("database.db");
    13→
    14→sqlgen::drop<Person>(conn).value();
    15→```
    16→
    17→This generates the following SQL:
    18→
    19→```sql
    20→DROP TABLE "Person";
    21→```
    22→
    23→Note that `conn` is actually a connection wrapped into an `sqlgen::Result<...>`.
    24→This means you can use monadic error handling and fit this into a single line:
    25→
    26→```cpp
    27→// sqlgen::Result<Ref<Connection>>
    28→const auto result = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("database.db").and_then(
    29→                        sqlgen::drop<Person>);
    30→```
    31→
    32→Please refer to the documentation on `sqlgen::Result<...>` for more information on error handling.
    33→
    34→### With `if_exists` clause
    35→
    36→Drop a table only if it exists:
    37→
    38→```cpp
    39→using namespace sqlgen;
    40→
    41→const auto query = drop<Person> | if_exists;
    42→
    43→query(conn).value();
    44→```
    45→
    46→This generates the following SQL:
    47→
    48→```sql
    49→DROP TABLE IF EXISTS "Person";
    50→```
    51→
    52→You can also use monadic error handling here:
    53→
    54→```cpp
    55→using namespace sqlgen;
    56→
    57→const auto query = drop<Person> | if_exists;
    58→
    59→// sqlgen::Result<Ref<Connection>>
    60→const auto result = sqlite::connect("database.db").and_then(query);
    61→```
    62→
    63→## Example: Full Query Composition
    64→
    65→```cpp
    66→using namespace sqlgen;
    67→
    68→const auto query = drop<Person> | if_exists;
    69→
    70→const auto result = query(conn);
    71→
    72→if (!result) {
    73→    // Error handling
    74→}
    75→```
    76→
    77→This generates the following SQL:
    78→
    79→```sql
    80→DROP TABLE IF EXISTS "Person";
    81→```
    82→
    83→It is strongly recommended that you use `using namespace sqlgen`. However,
    84→if you do not want to do that, you can rewrite the example above as follows:
    85→
    86→```cpp
    87→const auto query = sqlgen::drop<Person> | sqlgen::if_exists;
    88→
    89→const auto result = query(conn);
    90→```
    91→
    92→## Notes
    93→
    94→- The `if_exists` clause is optional - if omitted, the query will fail if the table doesn't exist
    95→- The `Result<Ref<Connection>>` type provides error handling; use `.value()` to extract the result (will throw an exception if there's an error) or handle errors as needed or refer to the documentation on `sqlgen::Result<...>` for other forms of error handling.
    96→- The table name is derived from the struct name (e.g., `Person` becomes `"Person"` in SQL)

    19→/// The concept any connection needs to implements.
    20→template <class ConnType>
    21→concept is_connection = requires(
    22→    ConnType c, std::string _sql, dynamic::Statement _stmt,
    23→    dynamic::SelectFrom _select_from, dynamic::Insert _insert,
    24→    const dynamic::Write& _write, std::vector<internal::MockTable> _data) {
    25→  /// Begins a transaction.
    26→  { c.begin_transaction() } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    27→
    28→  /// Commits a transaction.
    29→  { c.commit() } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    30→
    31→  /// Executes a statement.
    32→  { c.execute(_sql) } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    33→
    34→  /// Inserts data into the database using the INSERT statement.
    35→  /// More minimal approach than write, but can be used inside transactions.
    36→  {
    37→    c.insert(_insert, _data.begin(), _data.end())
    38→  } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    39→
    40→  /// Reads the results of a SelectFrom statement.
    41→  {
    42→    c.template read<std::vector<internal::MockTable>>(_select_from)
    43→  } -> std::same_as<Result<std::vector<internal::MockTable>>>;
    44→
    45→  /// Commits a transaction.
    46→  { c.rollback() } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    47→
    48→  /// Transpiles a statement to a particular SQL dialect.
    49→  { c.to_sql(_stmt) } -> std::same_as<std::string>;
    50→
    51→  /// Starts the write operation.
    52→  { c.start_write(_write) } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    53→
    54→  /// Ends the write operation and thus commits the results.
    55→  { c.end_write() } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    56→
    57→  /// Writes data into a table.
    58→  { c.write(_data.begin(), _data.end()) } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    59→};
    60→
    61→}  // namespace sqlgen

1→# `sqlgen::insert`
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen::insert` interface provides a type-safe way to insert data from C++ containers or ranges into a SQL database. Unlike `sqlgen::write`, it does not create tables automatically and is designed to be used within transactions. It's particularly useful when you need fine-grained control over table creation and transaction boundaries. 
     4→
     5→In particular, `sqlgen::insert` is the recommended way whenever you want to insert data into several tables that depend on each other, meaning that either all inserts should succeed or none of them.
     6→
     7→## Usage
     8→
     9→### Basic Insert
    10→
    11→Insert a container of objects into a database:
    12→
    13→```cpp
    14→const auto people = std::vector<Person>({
    15→    Person{.id = 0, .first_name = "Homer", .last_name = "Simpson", .age = 45},
    16→    Person{.id = 1, .first_name = "Bart", .last_name = "Simpson", .age = 10}
    17→});
    18→
    19→// Using with a connection reference
    20→const auto conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect();
    21→sqlgen::insert(conn, people);
    22→```
    23→
    24→This generates the following SQL:
    25→
    26→```sql
    27→INSERT INTO "Person" ("id", "first_name", "last_name", "age") VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?);
    28→```
    29→
    30→Note that `conn` is actually a connection wrapped into an `sqlgen::Result<...>`.
    31→This means you can use monadic error handling and fit this into a single line:
    32→
    33→```cpp
    34→// sqlgen::Result<Ref<Connection>>
    35→const auto result = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("database.db").and_then(
    36→                        sqlgen::insert(people));
    37→```
    38→
    39→Please refer to the documentation on `sqlgen::Result<...>` for more information on error handling.
    40→
    41→### With `Result<Ref<Connection>>`
    42→
    43→Handle connection creation and insertion in a single chain:
    44→
    45→```cpp
    46→sqlgen::sqlite::connect("database.db")
    47→    .and_then(sqlgen::insert(people))
    48→    .value();
    49→```
    50→
    51→### With Iterators
    52→
    53→Insert a range of objects using iterators:
    54→
    55→```cpp
    56→std::vector<Person> people = /* ... */;
    57→sqlgen::insert(conn, people.begin(), people.end());
    58→```
    59→
    60→### With Reference Wrapper
    61→
    62→Insert data using a reference wrapper to avoid copying:
    63→
    64→```cpp
    65→const auto people = std::vector<Person>(/* ... */);
    66→sqlgen::sqlite::connect("database.db")
    67→    .and_then(sqlgen::insert(std::ref(people)))
    68→    .value();
    69→```
    70→
    71→### With Replacement
    72→
    73→Replace existing rows:
    74→
    75→```cpp
    76→const auto people1 = std::vector<Person>({
    77→    Person{.id = 0, .first_name = "Homer", .last_name = "Simpson", .age = 45},
    78→    Person{.id = 1, .first_name = "Bart", .last_name = "Simpson", .age = 10}
    79→});
    80→
    81→const auto people2 = std::vector<Person>({
    82→    Person{.id = 1, .first_name = "Bartholomew", .last_name = "Simpson", .age = 10}
    83→});
    84→
    85→using namespace sqlgen;
    86→
    87→const auto result = sqlite::connect()
    88→    .and_then(create_table<Person> | if_not_exists)
    89→    .and_then(insert(std::ref(people1)))
    90→    .and_then(insert_or_replace(std::ref(people2)))
    91→    .value();
    92→```
    93→
    94→This generates the following SQL:
    95→
    96→```sql
    97→CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "Person" (
    98→    "id" INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    99→    "first_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
   100→    "last_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
   101→    "age" INTEGER NOT NULL
   102→);
   103→INSERT INTO "Person" ("id", "first_name", "last_name", "age") VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?);
   104→INSERT INTO "Person" ("id", "first_name", "last_name", "age") VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)
   105→ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET
   106→  id=excluded.id,
   107→  first_name=excluded.first_name,
   108→  last_name=excluded.last_name,
   109→  age=excluded.age;
   110→```
   111→
   112→The SQL generated by the PostgreSQL backend for `insert_or_replace(...)` is similar. The MySQL backend generates `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` instead:
   113→```sql
   114→...
   115→INSERT INTO `Person` (`id`, `first_name`, `last_name`, `age`) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)
   116→ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE
   117→  id=VALUES(id),
   118→  first_name=VALUES(first_name),
   119→  last_name=VALUES(last_name),
   120→  age=VALUES(age);
   121→```
   122→
   123→## Example: Full Transaction Usage
   124→
   125→Here's a complete example showing how to use `insert` within a transaction:
   126→
   127→```cpp
   128→using namespace sqlgen;
   129→
   130→const auto result = sqlite::connect()
   131→    .and_then(begin_transaction)
   132→    .and_then(create_table<Person> | if_not_exists)
   133→    .and_then(insert(std::ref(people)))
   134→    .and_then(commit)
   135→    .value();
   136→```
   137→
   138→This generates the following SQL:
   139→
   140→```sql
   141→BEGIN TRANSACTION;
   142→CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "Person" (
   143→    "id" INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
   144→    "first_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
   145→    "last_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
   146→    "age" INTEGER NOT NULL
   147→);
   148→INSERT INTO "Person" ("id", "first_name", "last_name", "age") VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?);
   149→COMMIT;
   150→```
   151→
   152→## Example: Multi-Table Insert with Dependencies
   153→
   154→Here's an example showing how to insert related data into multiple tables within a single transaction:
   155→
   156→```cpp
   157→struct Person {
   158→  sqlgen::PrimaryKey<uint32_t> id;
   159→  std::string first_name;
   160→  std::string last_name;
   161→  int age;
   162→};
   163→
   164→struct Children {
   165→  uint32_t id_parent;
   166→  sqlgen::PrimaryKey<uint32_t> id_child;
   167→};
   168→
   169→// Parent records
   170→const auto people = std::vector<Person>({
   171→    Person{.id = 0, .first_name = "Homer", .last_name = "Simpson", .age = 45},
   172→    Person{.id = 1, .first_name = "Bart", .last_name = "Simpson", .age = 10},
   173→    Person{.id = 2, .first_name = "Lisa", .last_name = "Simpson", .age = 8},
   174→    Person{.id = 3, .first_name = "Maggie", .last_name = "Simpson", .age = 0}
   175→});
   176→
   177→// Child relationships
   178→const auto children = std::vector<Children>({
   179→    Children{.id_parent = 0, .id_child = 1},  // Homer -> Bart
   180→    Children{.id_parent = 0, .id_child = 2},  // Homer -> Lisa
   181→    Children{.id_parent = 0, .id_child = 3}   // Homer -> Maggie
   182→});
   183→
   184→using namespace sqlgen;
   185→
   186→// All inserts are wrapped in a single transaction
   187→const auto result = postgres::connect(credentials)
   188→    .and_then(begin_transaction)
   189→    .and_then(create_table<Person> | if_not_exists)
   190→    .and_then(create_table<Children> | if_not_exists)
   191→    .and_then(insert(std::ref(people)))    // Insert people first
   192→    .and_then(insert(std::ref(children)))  // Then insert relationships
   193→    .and_then(commit)
   194→    .value();
   195→```
   196→
   197→This generates the following SQL:
   198→
   199→```sql
   200→BEGIN TRANSACTION;
   201→CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "Person" (
   202→    "id" INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
   203→    "first_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
   204→    "last_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
   205→    "age" INTEGER NOT NULL
   206→);
   207→CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "Children" (
   208→    "id_parent" INTEGER NOT NULL,
   209→    "id_child" INTEGER PRIMARY KEY
   210→);
   211→INSERT INTO "Person" ("id", "first_name", "last_name", "age") VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?);
   212→INSERT INTO "Children" ("id_parent", "id_child") VALUES (?, ?);
   213→COMMIT;
   214→```
   215→
   216→In this example, we insert both parent records and their relationships to children. If any insert fails, the entire transaction is rolled back, ensuring data consistency. This is crucial when dealing with related data across multiple tables.
   217→
   218→## Comparison with `sqlgen::write`
   219→
   220→While both `insert` and `write` can be used to add data to a database, they serve different purposes:
   221→
   222→### `sqlgen::write`
   223→- Automatically creates tables if they don't exist
   224→- Uses optimized bulk insert methods (e.g., PostgreSQL's COPY command)
   225→- More convenient for simple use cases
   226→- Faster for bulk inserts
   227→- Cannot be used within transactions
   228→- Best for single-table operations with no dependencies
   229→
   230→### `sqlgen::insert`
   231→- Does not create tables automatically
   232→- Uses standard INSERT statements
   233→- Designed to be used within transactions
   234→- More control over transaction boundaries
   235→- Better for complex operations requiring transaction support
   236→- Essential for multi-table operations with dependencies
   237→- Guarantees atomicity across multiple tables
   238→- Recommended when data consistency across tables is critical
   239→
   240→## Notes
   241→
   242→- The `Result<Ref<Connection>>` type provides error handling; use `.value()` to extract the result (will throw an exception if there's an error) or handle errors as needed
   243→- The function has several overloads:
   244→  1. Takes a connection reference and iterators
   245→  2. Takes a `Result<Ref<Connection>>` and iterators
   246→  3. Takes a connection and a container directly
   247→  4. Takes a connection and a reference wrapper to a container
   248→- Unlike `write`, `insert` does not create tables automatically - you must create tables separately using `create_table`
   249→- The insert operation is atomic within a transaction
   250→- When using reference wrappers (`std::ref`), the data is not copied, which can be more efficient for large datasets

1→# `sqlgen::insert`
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen::insert` interface provides a type-safe way to insert data from C++ containers or ranges into a SQL database. Unlike `sqlgen::write`, it does not create tables automatically and is designed to be used within transactions. It's particularly useful when you need fine-grained control over table creation and transaction boundaries. 
     4→
     5→In particular, `sqlgen::insert` is the recommended way whenever you want to insert data into several tables that depend on each other, meaning that either all inserts should succeed or none of them.
     6→
     7→## Usage
     8→
     9→### Basic Insert
    10→
    11→Insert a container of objects into a database:
    12→
    13→```cpp
    14→const auto people = std::vector<Person>({
    15→    Person{.id = 0, .first_name = "Homer", .last_name = "Simpson", .age = 45},
    16→    Person{.id = 1, .first_name = "Bart", .last_name = "Simpson", .age = 10}
    17→});
    18→
    19→// Using with a connection reference
    20→const auto conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect();
    21→sqlgen::insert(conn, people);
    22→```
    23→
    24→This generates the following SQL:
    25→
    26→```sql
    27→INSERT INTO "Person" ("id", "first_name", "last_name", "age") VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?);
    28→```
    29→
    30→Note that `conn` is actually a connection wrapped into an `sqlgen::Result<...>`.
    31→This means you can use monadic error handling and fit this into a single line:
    32→
    33→```cpp
    34→// sqlgen::Result<Ref<Connection>>
    35→const auto result = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("database.db").and_then(
    36→                        sqlgen::insert(people));
    37→```

    39→Please refer to the documentation on `sqlgen::Result<...>` for more information on error handling.

1→# String Operations
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen` library provides a set of string functions for use in queries. These functions are type-safe and map to the appropriate SQL operations for the target database.
     4→
     5→## Motivating Example
     6→Suppose you want to create a report of people with their full names in uppercase, and also want to trim any whitespace from their last names:
     7→
     8→```cpp
     9→struct PersonReport {
    10→  std::string full_name;
    11→  std::string last_name_trimmed;
    12→};
    13→
    14→const auto get_reports =
    15→    select_from<Person>(
    16→        concat(upper("last_name"_c), ", ", "first_name"_c).as<"full_name">(),
    17→        trim("last_name"_c).as<"last_name_trimmed">()
    18→    )
    19→    | to<std::vector<PersonReport>>;
    20→```
    21→
    22→This query produces a list of people with their full names in the format "LASTNAME, Firstname" (with the last name in uppercase) and ensures the last name has no leading or trailing whitespace.
    23→
    24→## String Functions
    25→
    26→### `length`
    27→Returns the length of a string.
    28→
    29→```cpp
    30→length(trim("first_name"_c)) | as<"length_first_name">
    31→```
    32→
    33→### `lower` / `upper`
    34→Converts a string to lowercase or uppercase.
    35→
    36→```cpp
    37→lower("first_name"_c) | as<"first_name_lower">
    38→upper("first_name"_c) | as<"first_name_upper">
    39→```
    40→
    41→### `ltrim`, `rtrim`, `trim`
    42→Removes whitespace (or a specified character) from the left, right, or both sides of a string.
    43→
    44→```cpp
    45→ltrim("first_name"_c) | as<"ltrimmed_name">
    46→rtrim("last_name"_c) | as<"rtrimmed_name">
    47→trim("nickname"_c) | as<"trimmed_nickname">
    48→// With custom characters:
    49→ltrim("field"_c, "_ ") | as<"ltrimmed_field">
    50→```
    51→
    52→### `replace`
    53→Replaces all occurrences of a substring with another substring.
    54→
    55→```cpp
    56→replace("first_name"_c, "Bart", "Hugo") | as<"first_name_replaced">
    57→```
    58→
    59→### `concat`
    60→Concatenates multiple strings or expressions.
    61→
    62→```cpp
    63→concat("first_name"_c, " ", "last_name"_c) | as<"full_name">
    64→concat(upper("last_name"_c), ", ", "first_name"_c) | as<"full_name">
    65→```

    17→namespace sqlgen {

    19→/// The concept any connection needs to implements.
    20→template <class ConnType>
    21→concept is_connection = requires(
    22→    ConnType c, std::string _sql, dynamic::Statement _stmt,
    23→    dynamic::SelectFrom _select_from, dynamic::Insert _insert,
    24→    const dynamic::Write& _write, std::vector<internal::MockTable> _data) {
    25→  /// Begins a transaction.
    26→  { c.begin_transaction() } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    27→
    28→  /// Commits a transaction.
    29→  { c.commit() } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    30→
    31→  /// Executes a statement.
    32→  { c.execute(_sql) } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    33→
    34→  /// Inserts data into the database using the INSERT statement.
    35→  /// More minimal approach than write, but can be used inside transactions.
    36→  {
    37→    c.insert(_insert, _data.begin(), _data.end())
    38→  } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    39→
    40→  /// Reads the results of a SelectFrom statement.
    41→  {
    42→    c.template read<std::vector<internal::MockTable>>(_select_from)
    43→  } -> std::same_as<Result<std::vector<internal::MockTable>>>;
    44→
    45→  /// Commits a transaction.
    46→  { c.rollback() } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    47→
    48→  /// Transpiles a statement to a particular SQL dialect.
    49→  { c.to_sql(_stmt) } -> std::same_as<std::string>;
    50→
    51→  /// Starts the write operation.
    52→  { c.start_write(_write) } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    53→
    54→  /// Ends the write operation and thus commits the results.
    55→  { c.end_write() } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    56→
    57→  /// Writes data into a table.
    58→  { c.write(_data.begin(), _data.end()) } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    59→};
    60→
    61→}  // namespace sqlgen

    19→/// The concept any connection needs to implements.
    20→template <class ConnType>
    21→concept is_connection = requires(
    22→    ConnType c, std::string _sql, dynamic::Statement _stmt,
    23→    dynamic::SelectFrom _select_from, dynamic::Insert _insert,
    24→    const dynamic::Write& _write, std::vector<internal::MockTable> _data) {
    25→  /// Begins a transaction.
    26→  { c.begin_transaction() } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    27→
    28→  /// Commits a transaction.
    29→  { c.commit() } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    30→
    31→  /// Executes a statement.
    32→  { c.execute(_sql) } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    33→
    34→  /// Inserts data into the database using the INSERT statement.
    35→  /// More minimal approach than write, but can be used inside transactions.
    36→  {
    37→    c.insert(_insert, _data.begin(), _data.end())
    38→  } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    39→
    40→  /// Reads the results of a SelectFrom statement.
    41→  {
    42→    c.template read<std::vector<internal::MockTable>>(_select_from)
    43→  } -> std::same_as<Result<std::vector<internal::MockTable>>>;
    44→
    45→  /// Commits a transaction.
    46→  { c.rollback() } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    47→
    48→  /// Transpiles a statement to a particular SQL dialect.
    49→  { c.to_sql(_stmt) } -> std::same_as<std::string>;
    50→
    51→  /// Starts the write operation.
    52→  { c.start_write(_write) } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    53→
    54→  /// Ends the write operation and thus commits the results.
    55→  { c.end_write() } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    56→
    57→  /// Writes data into a table.
    58→  { c.write(_data.begin(), _data.end()) } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    59→};

1→# `sqlgen::drop` 
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen::drop` interface provides a type-safe way to drop tables from a SQL database. It supports the `if_exists` clause to handle cases where the table may not exist.
     4→
     5→## Usage
     6→
     7→### Basic Drop
     8→
     9→Drop a table:
    10→
    11→```cpp
    12→const auto conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("database.db");
    13→
    14→sqlgen::drop<Person>(conn).value();
    15→```
    16→
    17→This generates the following SQL:
    18→
    19→```sql
    20→DROP TABLE "Person";
    21→```
    22→
    23→Note that `conn` is actually a connection wrapped into an `sqlgen::Result<...>`.
    24→This means you can use monadic error handling and fit this into a single line:
    25→
    26→```cpp
    27→// sqlgen::Result<Ref<Connection>>
    28→const auto result = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("database.db").and_then(
    29→                        sqlgen::drop<Person>);
    30→```
    31→
    32→Please refer to the documentation on `sqlgen::Result<...>` for more information on error handling.
    33→
    34→### With `if_exists` clause
    35→
    36→Drop a table only if it exists:
    37→
    38→```cpp
    39→using namespace sqlgen;
    40→
    41→const auto query = drop<Person> | if_exists;
    42→
    43→query(conn).value();
    44→```
    45→
    46→This generates the following SQL:
    47→
    48→```sql
    49→DROP TABLE IF EXISTS "Person";
    50→```
    51→
    52→You can also use monadic error handling here:
    53→
    54→```cpp
    55→using namespace sqlgen;
    56→
    57→const auto query = drop<Person> | if_exists;
    58→
    59→// sqlgen::Result<Ref<Connection>>
    60→const auto result = sqlite::connect("database.db").and_then(query);
    61→```
    62→
    63→## Example: Full Query Composition
    64→
    65→```cpp
    66→using namespace sqlgen;
    67→
    68→const auto query = drop<Person> | if_exists;
    69→
    70→const auto result = query(conn);
    71→
    72→if (!result) {
    73→    // Error handling
    74→}
    75→```
    76→
    77→This generates the following SQL:
    78→
    79→```sql
    80→DROP TABLE IF EXISTS "Person";
    81→```
    82→
    83→It is strongly recommended that you use `using namespace sqlgen`. However,
    84→if you do not want to do that, you can rewrite the example above as follows:
    85→
    86→```cpp
    87→const auto query = sqlgen::drop<Person> | sqlgen::if_exists;
    88→
    89→const auto result = query(conn);
    90→```
    91→
    92→## Notes
    93→
    94→- The `if_exists` clause is optional - if omitted, the query will fail if the table doesn't exist
    95→- The `Result<Ref<Connection>>` type provides error handling; use `.value()` to extract the result (will throw an exception if there's an error) or handle errors as needed or refer to the documentation on `sqlgen::Result<...>` for other forms of error handling.
    96→- The table name is derived from the struct name (e.g., `Person` becomes `"Person"` in SQL)
    97→

    22→    ConnType c, std::string _sql, dynamic::Statement _stmt,
    23→    dynamic::SelectFrom _select_from, dynamic::Insert _insert,
    24→    const dynamic::Write& _write, std::vector<internal::MockTable> _data) {
    25→  /// Begins a transaction.
    26→  { c.begin_transaction() } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    27→
    28→  /// Commits a transaction.
    29→  { c.commit() } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    30→
    31→  /// Executes a statement.
    32→  { c.execute(_sql) } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    33→
    34→  /// Inserts data into the database using the INSERT statement.
    35→  /// More minimal approach than write, but can be used inside transactions.
    36→  {
    37→    c.insert(_insert, _data.begin(), _data.end())
    38→  } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    39→
    40→  /// Reads the results of a SelectFrom statement.
    41→  {
    42→    c.template read<std::vector<internal::MockTable>>(_select_from)
    43→  } -> std::same_as<Result<std::vector<internal::MockTable>>>;
    44→
    45→  /// Commits a transaction.
    46→  { c.rollback() } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    47→
    48→  /// Transpiles a statement to a particular SQL dialect.
    49→  { c.to_sql(_stmt) } -> std::same_as<std::string>;

    52→  { c.start_write(_write) } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;

    55→  { c.end_write() } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;
    56→

    58→  { c.write(_data.begin(), _data.end()) } -> std::same_as<Result<Nothing>>;

1→# `sqlgen::create_as` 
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen::create_as` interface provides a type-safe way to create tables and views from SELECT queries in a SQL database. It supports both `CREATE TABLE AS` and `CREATE VIEW AS` syntax, with options for `if_not_exists` and `or_replace` clauses.
     4→
     5→## Usage
     6→
     7→### Basic Create Table As
     8→
     9→Create a table from a SELECT query:
    10→
    11→```cpp
    12→using namespace sqlgen;
    13→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    14→
    15→const auto names_query = select_from<Person>("first_name"_c, "last_name"_c);
    16→const auto get_names = create_as<Name>(names_query);
    17→
    18→get_names(conn).value();
    19→```
    20→
    21→This generates the following SQL:
    22→
    23→```sql
    24→CREATE TABLE "Name" AS SELECT "first_name", "last_name" FROM "Person";
    25→```
    26→
    27→### With `if_not_exists` clause
    28→
    29→Create a table only if it doesn't exist:
    30→
    31→```cpp
    32→using namespace sqlgen;
    33→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    34→
    35→const auto names_query = select_from<Person>("first_name"_c, "last_name"_c);
    36→const auto get_names = create_as<Name>(names_query) | if_not_exists;
    37→
    38→get_names(conn).value();
    39→```
    40→
    41→This generates the following SQL:
    42→
    43→```sql
    44→CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "Name" AS SELECT "first_name", "last_name" FROM "Person";
    45→```
    46→
    47→### Create View As
    48→
    49→Create a view from a SELECT query:
    50→
    51→```cpp
    52→using namespace sqlgen;
    53→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    54→
    55→const auto names_query = select_from<Person>("first_name"_c, "last_name"_c);
    56→const auto get_names = create_or_replace_view_as<Name>(names_query);
    57→
    58→get_names(conn).value();
    59→```
    60→
    61→This generates the following SQL:
    62→
    63→```sql
    64→CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW "NAMES" AS SELECT "first_name", "last_name" FROM "PEOPLE";
    65→```
    66→
    67→Note: Views require the struct to have `static constexpr bool is_view = true;`. Optionally, you can specify a custom name using `static constexpr const char* viewname = "VIEW_NAME";` or `static constexpr const char* tablename = "VIEW_NAME";` (both work the same way for views).
    68→
    69→## Example: Full Query Composition
    70→
    71→```cpp
    72→using namespace sqlgen;
    73→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    74→
    75→// Define the source data structure
    76→struct Person {
    77→  sqlgen::PrimaryKey<uint32_t> id;
    78→  std::string first_name;
    79→  std::string last_name;
    80→  int age;
    81→};
    82→
    83→// Define the target structure for the new table/view
    84→struct Name {
    85→  std::string first_name;
    86→  std::string last_name;
    87→};
    88→
    89→// Create a SELECT query
    90→const auto names_query = select_from<Person>("first_name"_c, "last_name"_c);
    91→
    92→// Create table as query
    93→const auto create_table_query = create_as<Name>(names_query) | if_not_exists;
    94→
    95→// Execute the query
    96→const auto result = create_table_query(conn);
    97→
    98→if (!result) {
    99→    // Error handling
   100→}
   101→```
   102→
   103→This generates the following SQL:
   104→
   105→```sql
   106→CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "Name" AS SELECT "first_name", "last_name" FROM "Person";
   107→```
   108→
   109→## View Creation
   110→
   111→To create views, your struct must be marked as a view:
   112→
   113→```cpp
   114→struct Name {
   115→  static constexpr bool is_view = true;
   116→  // Optionally specify a custom name
   117→  static constexpr const char* viewname = "NAMES";  // or tablename = "NAMES"
   118→  
   119→  std::string first_name;
   120→  std::string last_name;
   121→};
   122→```
   123→
   124→Then use `create_or_replace_view_as`:
   125→
   126→```cpp
   127→const auto names_query = select_from<Person>("first_name"_c, "last_name"_c);
   128→const auto get_names = create_or_replace_view_as<Name>(names_query);
   129→
   130→get_names(conn).value();
   131→```
   132→
   133→## Database-Specific Behavior
   134→
   135→### MySQL
   136→
   137→MySQL supports both `CREATE TABLE AS` and `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW AS`:
   138→
   139→```sql
   140→-- Table creation
   141→CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS `Name` AS SELECT `first_name`, `last_name` FROM `Person`;
   142→
   143→-- View creation  
   144→CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW `NAMES` AS SELECT `first_name`, `last_name` FROM `PEOPLE`;
   145→```
   146→
   147→### PostgreSQL
   148→
   149→PostgreSQL supports both `CREATE TABLE AS` and `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW AS`:
   150→
   151→```sql
   152→-- Table creation
   153→CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "Name" AS SELECT "first_name", "last_name" FROM "Person";
   154→
   155→-- View creation
   156→CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW "NAMES" AS SELECT "first_name", "last_name" FROM "PEOPLE";
   157→```
   158→
   159→### SQLite
   160→
   161→SQLite has different view creation behavior:
   162→
   163→```sql
   164→-- Table creation
   165→CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "Name" AS SELECT "first_name", "last_name" FROM "Person";
   166→
   167→-- View creation - SQLite does NOT support CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW
   168→-- Instead, it uses CREATE VIEW IF NOT EXISTS
   169→CREATE VIEW IF NOT EXISTS "NAMES" AS SELECT "first_name", "last_name" FROM "PEOPLE";
   170→```
   171→
   172→**Important**: SQLite does not support `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW`. Do not use `create_or_replace_view_as` with SQLite.
   173→
   174→## Monadic Error Handling
   175→
   176→Like other sqlgen operations, `create_as` supports monadic error handling:
   177→
   178→```cpp
   179→using namespace sqlgen;
   180→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
   181→
   182→const auto names_query = select_from<Person>("first_name"_c, "last_name"_c);
   183→const auto get_names = create_as<Name>(names_query);
   184→
   185→// sqlgen::Result<std::vector<Name>>
   186→const auto result = sqlite::connect("database.db")
   187→                       .and_then(drop<Name> | if_exists)
   188→                       .and_then(drop<Person> | if_exists)
   189→                       .and_then(write(std::ref(people)))
   190→                       .and_then(get_names)
   191→                       .and_then(sqlgen::read<std::vector<Name>>);
   192→```
   193→
   194→## Notes
   195→
   196→- The `if_not_exists` clause is optional - if omitted, the query will fail if the table already exists
   197→- Views require `static constexpr bool is_view = true;` in the struct definition
   198→- Custom names can be specified using either `viewname` or `tablename` - they work identically for tables and views
   199→- The `Result<Ref<Connection>>` type provides error handling; use `.value()` to extract the result (will throw an exception if there's an error) or handle errors as needed
   200→- The table/view name is derived from the struct name (e.g., `Name` becomes `"Name"` in SQL) unless overridden by `tablename` or `viewname`
   201→- The SELECT query must be convertible to the output struct type
   202→- All columns from the SELECT query must have corresponding fields in the target struct
   203→- **SQLite Limitation**: SQLite does not support `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW` - use `create_as<ViewType>(query) | if_not_exists` for SQLite compatibility
   204→- **MySQL/PostgreSQL**: Both support `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW` and work with `create_or_replace_view_as`
